title: AI That Uses Your Computer: What Screen-Control Agents Can and Cannot Do
summary: Computer-use agents can now click, type, and navigate your screen. Here is what they actually automate today, where they fail, and what to check before giving one your credentials.
before: You describe a task in words, and the AI gives you instructions to follow yourself. The AI never touches your screen.
after: You describe a task, and the agent sees your screen, moves the mouse, types, and completes the workflow autonomously.
body:
Something shifted in early 2026: AI agents stopped just answering questions and started doing things on your computer. These systems can see your screen, move your mouse, click buttons, fill forms, and complete multi-step tasks while you watch. The promise is simple: describe what you want done, and the agent does it. The reality is more complicated.

## How Computer-Use Agents Work

A **computer-use agent** operates through a perception-action loop. It takes a screenshot, sends it to a vision model that interprets what is on screen, then executes an action like clicking or typing, and repeats. Unlike traditional automation tools that follow rigid scripts, these agents can adapt when layouts change or unexpected pop-ups appear.

The major players work a little differently under the hood. Claude's browser extension and computer use API rely on screenshot analysis combined with reasoning. OpenAI's approach, now integrated into ChatGPT Agent after the standalone Operator product was shut down in August 2025, uses a similar vision-and-action cycle. Google's current offering is not a standalone agent at all: as of 2026-07-20, its experimental Project Mariner has been discontinued and folded into other products. Google shut Mariner down as a standalone product on May 4, 2026, after a roughly 17-month run, moving its capabilities into Gemini Agent and Chrome's Auto Browse feature. Worth clearing up a common misconception: Mariner was a screenshot-and-computer-vision agent that interpreted rendered pages visually the way a human does, not a DOM-first tool. Chrome Auto Browse, built on Gemini 3, now carries forward that multi-step browsing behavior for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the US, running inside the browser and sessions you are already logged into. Open-source options like Browser Use, with over 90,000 GitHub stars, let you run similar capabilities with your choice of underlying model.

## What They Can Actually Do Today

These agents genuinely work for certain tasks. Repetitive browser work like filling forms, collecting data from dashboards, and organizing files are their sweet spot. They can navigate websites, compare prices, schedule appointments, and handle multi-step research workflows. Chrome Auto Browse, for example, advertises hotel and flight research across flexible dates, appointment scheduling, online form filling from a PDF, subscription management, and budget-capped shopping.

Claude's browser automation includes a confirmation step for major actions like bulk deletion or unsubscribing. ChatGPT Agent lets you schedule recurring tasks and access them across devices. For developers, these tools can verify front-end implementations by clicking through an app the way a real user would.

## Where They Fail

The limitations are consistent across products. CAPTCHAs stop them cold. Two-factor authentication requires you to step in. Complex JavaScript interfaces, drag-and-drop functionality, and intricate calendar systems still confuse agents regularly. Payment transactions and banking are off-limits by design, or at minimum require you to explicitly confirm.

Speed is another issue. Browser automation is inherently slow because it must wait for pages to load, JavaScript to execute, and the DOM to render. An agent completing a task that takes you 30 seconds might need several minutes of screenshot-analyze-click cycles. This latency was one of the reasons Google retired Mariner as a standalone product: the screenshot-based approach was compute-intensive and slow at scale, while the industry shifted toward faster, more reliable code-level and API-first agents.

Benchmark scores tell the story, though they need to be read carefully. On OSWorld, a standard benchmark of real desktop tasks, the human baseline sits around 72%, and for most of 2024 and 2025 leading agents scored well below that. As of 2026-07-20, the best-tuned system setups on the public leaderboard reach the mid-80s, while frontier base models land roughly in the low-to-mid 70s. Even at the top of the board, that means one in six or so attempts fails, and independent researchers caution that leaderboard numbers can overstate real-world reliability. On longer, multi-step workflows, success rates drop sharply.

## The Security Question

This is where things get serious. A computer-use agent can click buttons, delete files, send emails, and execute commands using your credentials. Every session you are logged into, the agent can access.

**Prompt injection** is the primary concern. An attacker hides instructions on a webpage, invisible to you but readable by the agent. Your agent visits the page, follows those hidden instructions as if you typed them, and acts using your active sessions. In August 2025, researchers found that hidden text on a webpage caused an agent to extract a user's email and one-time passcode. No malware required, just text on a page.

The platforms building these tools have added safeguards. Claude requires confirmation for high-impact actions and asks permission before accessing new apps. ChatGPT Agent uses "watch mode" requiring supervision on sensitive sites and refuses banking transactions entirely. Chrome Auto Browse is designed to pause and explicitly ask for confirmation before it does things like making a purchase, signing into accounts, or posting on social media, and asks permission before using Google Password Manager to log you in. But these measures reduce risk rather than eliminate it, and the vendors themselves say so.

## What to Check Before Trusting an Agent With Your Accounts

Before you let any computer-use agent access your logged-in sessions, ask these questions:

- **Does it sandbox actions?** Running agents in isolated environments like virtual machines or containers limits the blast radius if something goes wrong. Agents that act directly on the browser sessions you are logged into are a meaningfully harder safety problem than agents running in a throwaway VM.
- **What confirmation steps exist?** Look for products that pause before irreversible actions and let you review what the agent plans to do.
- **Can you audit what happened?** Some agents provide screenshots and logs of every action. Others do not. If you cannot review what the agent did, you cannot catch problems.
- **What sites should be off-limits?** Keep agents away from banking, email, and anything with stored payment methods until you have high confidence in the system.

Run any new agent manually at least three times before scheduling it to work autonomously. Introduce small variations and see if it recovers gracefully.

## Where This Is Heading

Computer-use agents are the least capable versions you will ever use, and that is both exciting and a reason for caution. The direction of travel is clear: rather than standalone agent products, the big platforms are embedding these capabilities directly into tools you already use, which is exactly what Google's Mariner-into-Chrome move signals. The technology is improving quickly, but as of 2026-07-20, treat these tools as powerful assistants that require supervision rather than autonomous workers you can fully trust with sensitive accounts.

For more context on how these agents fit into the broader landscape of AI systems that take action, see our explainer on agentic-ai-explained. The underlying models powering these agents continue to improve, as we covered in state-of-llms-q2-2026.
